report.tagline: The AI pair programmer built into VS Code and GitHub that suggests code, answers questions and now completes whole tasks as an agent.
report.simpleSummary: GitHub Copilot is an AI helper for programmers. As you type code, it guesses the next lines and you press Tab to accept. You can also chat with it about your code, or give it a task like 'fix this bug' and it writes the change and opens a pull request for you to review. It was the first AI coding tool used by millions, and it is owned by Microsoft.

overview.whatItDoes: Copilot helps developers write, understand and fix code faster. It works inside code editors like VS Code, JetBrains and Visual Studio, and on github.com. It started as autocomplete and now includes chat, an agent mode that edits many files, and a coding agent that works on GitHub issues by itself.
howItWorks: Code completion: as you type, grey text suggests the next line or block; press Tab to accept.
Copilot Chat: ask questions about your code, get explanations or tests, in the editor or on github.com.
Agent mode: describe a change and Copilot plans it, edits several files and runs commands, asking for approval.
Coding agent: assign a GitHub issue to Copilot; it works in the cloud and opens a pull request for review.
You can choose models from OpenAI, Anthropic and Google; stronger models use 'premium requests' that are limited per plan.
Companies control settings, block code that matches public code, and see usage dashboards.
overview.valueProposition: Write and ship code faster without leaving the tools and GitHub workflow your team already uses, with company-grade security.

coreFeatures.whatItDoes: Inline suggestions as you type, including 'next edit suggestions' that predict where you will edit next.
coreFeatures.whyItMatters: The original habit-forming feature; it is used many times an hour.

coreFeatures.whatItDoes: Ask questions, generate code and tests, and explain errors in the editor or on github.com.
coreFeatures.whyItMatters: Moves Copilot from typing help to a thinking partner.

coreFeatures.whatItDoes: Makes multi-file changes, runs terminal commands and fixes its own errors in the editor.
coreFeatures.whyItMatters: Matches what Cursor and Claude Code offer; key to keeping developers from switching.

coreFeatures.whatItDoes: Works on assigned GitHub issues in the background and opens pull requests.
coreFeatures.whyItMatters: Uses GitHub's unique position: it owns issues, pull requests and Actions.

coreFeatures.whatItDoes: Pick models from OpenAI, Anthropic and Google, and manage several coding agents from one place on GitHub.
coreFeatures.whyItMatters: Turns GitHub into the home for all coding agents, not just its own.

businessModel.summary: GitHub makes money from Copilot through monthly subscriptions per user, mostly from companies. Plans include a set number of 'premium requests' for advanced models and agents, and extra requests are billed by use. Copilot also makes GitHub's other paid products, like Enterprise and Actions, more valuable.

revenueStreams.detail: $19 and $39 per user a month; the biggest revenue source.
Pro at $10 and Pro+ at $39 a month.
$0.04 per extra request beyond plan limits.
Coding agent runs on Actions, which drives compute usage.
Sold alongside Azure and Microsoft enterprise deals.

businessModel.pricing: Free: limited completions and chats a month. Pro: $10 a month. Pro+: $39 a month. Business: $19 per user a month. Enterprise: $39 per user a month. Extra premium requests: $0.04 each. Free for verified students, teachers and popular open-source maintainers.
costDrivers: Model inference costs, including payments to OpenAI, Anthropic and Google
Compute for the coding agent in GitHub Actions
Engineering for editor plugins across VS Code, JetBrains, Visual Studio, Xcode and others
Free users and free student plans
businessModel.unitEconomics: A Business seat pays $19 a month. A light user who mostly uses completions may cost a few dollars in compute, so the seat is profitable. A heavy user running agent mode with top models all day could cost more than $19, which is why GitHub added premium request limits and $0.04 overage charges in 2025. Profit depends on the mix: many light users in a big company pay for the few heavy ones.

growth.moat: GitHub owns where code lives and where teams work together: repositories, issues, pull requests and Actions. Copilot can act on all of that directly. Enterprise contracts and security approvals make it the safe default. But the editor experience can be copied, and rivals like Cursor have moved faster on AI features.

competitors.name: Cursor
competitors.positioning: AI-first code editor, a fork of VS Code, loved for speed and agent features.
competitors.howThisProductDiffers: Cursor often ships AI features first and feels faster; Copilot is cheaper, works in many editors and has GitHub integration.

competitors.name: Claude Code (Anthropic)
competitors.positioning: Terminal-based coding agent that handles big tasks.
competitors.howThisProductDiffers: Claude Code is strong for autonomous work; Copilot offers Claude models inside its own product and GitHub workflow.

competitors.name: OpenAI Codex
competitors.positioning: Cloud coding agent and CLI from OpenAI.
competitors.howThisProductDiffers: Similar agent idea; Copilot has GitHub's repositories and enterprise trust.

competitors.name: Windsurf and Google Antigravity
competitors.howThisProductDiffers: Copilot has more enterprise customers; rivals compete on new agent experiences.

competitors.name: Amazon Q Developer
competitors.howThisProductDiffers: Q is strongest for AWS users; Copilot is broader and more widely used.

northStar.metric: Weekly accepted code changes per active developer (completions, edits and merged agent pull requests)
northStar.why: Accepted and merged code means Copilot did useful work that a developer chose to keep. It measures real value, not just usage. Guardrail metrics make sure growth does not come at the cost of trust, safety or margins.

pmLessons: Being first is not enough. Copilot started the category, but Cursor won many fans by moving faster.
Own the workflow. GitHub's issues and pull requests let Copilot do things editor-only tools cannot.
Pricing must match costs. Agent features cost more to run, so GitHub had to add usage limits, which upset users.
Enterprise trust is a growth engine. Security controls let Copilot spread through big companies.
Measure accepted work, not suggestions shown.

interviewQuestions.question: Cursor is winning developers who used to use Copilot. What would you do as Copilot PM?
interviewQuestions.hint: Find why they switch: speed, agent quality, UX. Use surveys and churn data. Prioritise fixes, use GitHub's unique strengths, and set a metric like switching rate.

interviewQuestions.question: How would you measure Copilot's impact on developer productivity?
interviewQuestions.hint: Mix output (PRs merged, cycle time), quality (bugs, reverts) and experience (surveys). Use test and control teams.

interviewQuestions.question: Should Copilot charge per seat or per use?
interviewQuestions.hint: Seat is simple for buyers; use matches cost. Consider hybrid with included requests. Think about heavy and light users and enterprise budgets.

interviewQuestions.question: Design the experience for assigning an issue to the Copilot coding agent.
interviewQuestions.hint: Walk through: picking issues, setting expectations, progress updates, review and feedback. Define success as merge rate and time saved.

interviewQuestions.question: Copilot lets users choose models from OpenAI, Anthropic and Google. Is that a good strategy?
interviewQuestions.hint: Pros: best model always, less dependency. Cons: cost, confusion, rivals gaining bargaining power. Suggest a smart default with an advanced option.
